title: Where hot music originated
summary: Brown says hot music began in New Orleans from plantation singing, riverfront roustabouts and church music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Where do you think hot music originated? Hot music? Or ragtime, or whatever you want.
All down in this particular section of country.
And what does that include? Does that include any particular states or only one, or what?

More so down in New Orleans. It was all through the plantations and things like that. The old Negroes out there, I used to many times when I was a kid go along the river, and these Negro roasterabouts would be sitting out on a cotton bale waiting for the boats. And they'd be singing. And they'd harmonize so beautifully, you know what I mean? Oh, you never heard anything like it in your life. I'd just sit around there and listen to them for hours. And they'd just sing until the boat was ready to be loaded. And they'd have to go to work then. But I'd sit around, and some of them would bring the instrument, some of them would have a banjo or something. Some of them would have a trumpet, an old batted up trumpet. And they'd play their tune, some popular number, like they think it should be played, you know, improvising and playing it in their way, their style. And like I heard a Negro one time in one of the churches playing an organ. And instead of playing the organ like you would ordinarily play, he'd make a lot of arpeggio notes, you know, on the basses. And he had a rhythm going of his own. It sounds just like an orchestra in those days, see? And that's his way of playing. But I think hot music originally started right down here in New Orleans. And it all drifted in here from the plantations, you know. You could find it like in Baton Rouge, all that center, you'd find music coming through there. And in New Orleans the same way. We'd all get ideas from all around that section. And then for harmony, we used to love to pass by these Negro churches and hear them sing.
